questions.q: How is absentee voting data reported, and what do I need to know when analyzing the statistics?
questions.a:
The WEC posts daily absentee ballot report spreadsheets leading up to an election. There are two spreadsheets generated by the system at 7:30 a.m. each day, one broken down by county and another by municipality. You can access those reports here: https://elections.wi.gov/statistics-data/absentee-statistics.

There are individual pages, based on the election, where the daily absentee reports are posted. To access a given election, go to that year and you’ll find what you need.

questions.q: What do the columns in the spreadsheet mean?
questions.a: The first three columns of numbers represent all absentee ballots. The last column (Column G) is for in-person absentee ballots and is a direct subset of the third column. (See more below for additional clarity).

questions.q: How should media report absentee voting numbers?
questions.a:
Members of the media should use column “F: Ballots Returned” when reporting how many people voted early, ahead of Election Day. This data includes all absentee ballots returned to the clerk either by mail, in person, or placed in a drop box. In addition, this data includes voters who cast a ballot during In-Person Absentee Voting (IPAV) hours.

Use column “G: In-person absentee” when reporting only on voters who went to a voting location ahead of Election Day, known as In-Person Absentee Voting (IPAV). NEVER add F & G columns together. Column G is a subset/filtered version of column F. Additional questions? Reach out to the Public Information Office at @email (https://elections.wi.gov/news-events/wisconsins-election-faqs).

questions.q: Does the data show the political party affiliation of voters requesting absentee ballots?
questions.a: No. This data doesn’t exist because Wisconsin does not register voters by political party.

questions.q: Where does the data come from?
questions.a:
The data is based on entries made by municipal clerks within Wisconsin’s statewide voter registration system. Note: More than 1,000 of the 1,850+ municipal clerks in Wisconsin do not have direct access to the system due to their size and rely on their county clerk or a neighboring clerk to enter data on their behalf.

The data also tracks requests and ballots, not voters. For example, some voters submit multiple requests for an absentee ballot or request a replacement ballot. In these instances, clerks only count one ballot per voter.  (https://elections.wi.gov/node/1231)

questions.q: What is the new USPS by mail voting rule, and how does it impact Wisconsin?
questions.a:
In March 2026, President Trump issued an Executive Order directing USPS to develop an administrative rule that would regulate federal absentee voting by mail. USPS finalized and published that rule on Wednesday, August 26, 2026. The rule applies nationwide to any state that uses the USPS to send or receive absentee ballots.

The rule proposed a system where all states would use a specific ballot envelope containing personalized barcodes for absentee voters. States would have to individually upload voter information for each by mail absentee voter (except military and overseas voters) into a USPS absentee voter portal prior to sending the absentee ballots out. Then, USPS would scan the barcodes on the envelopes to determine if the ballot can or cannot be delivered to the voter by USPS. Under the rule, which is now blocked by a federal court, USPS would not deliver any absentee ballots it could not verify through its portal.

You can read the full text of the rule here: https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-17238.pdf

USPS has also developed an FAQ for its rule that it issued before the rule was blocked. You can read that here, but please note it contains outdated information and the provisions of the rule described are not currently in effect: https://about.usps.com/what/government-services/election-mail/pdf/faq-usps-final-rule-ballot-mail-federal-elections.pdf

questions.q: Is the USPS rule currently in effect?
questions.a: No. On Thursday, August 27, a federal court entered an order blocking the rule, and USPS is currently unable to enforce it or compel states to comply with it.

questions.q: What did the court do?
questions.a: The federal court blocked all mandatory components of the USPS rule. The court said that while USPS could continue to build the portal and develop these systems, no state can be compelled to use them.

questions.q: Can USPS refuse to deliver absentee ballots if states don’t follow the rule?
questions.a: No. Because enforcement of the rule is currently blocked by a federal court, USPS must continue to mail absentee ballots as usual.

questions.q: Will Wisconsin comply with the rule even if it's not in effect?
questions.a:
No. Wisconsin cannot comply for several reasons. First, the USPS portal does not exist. USPS has given no indication of when or whether it will exist, and USPS has provided no training on how the portal will be used. The USPS rule is not a simple administrative change. It proposes a brand-new, highly complex, untested system involving new carrier envelope design, information coded into Intelligent Mail barcodes, a USPS-run database of voter information (input by clerks), none of which the Commission or clerks have been trained to develop or use. The USPS rule was developed and published in under five months, and USPS has not issued any training or explanation of how this system will actually work.

Second, the first batches of absentee ballots for the November election will be going out across the country starting the week of August 31, including in Wisconsin. It is too late for Wisconsin, or any state, to make significant changes to election law, policy, or procedure because voting is underway.

Finally, state and federal caselaw prohibit Wisconsin from making major changes in close proximity to an ongoing election. Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U.S. 1 (2006); Hawkins v. Wisconsin Elections Commission, 2020 WI 75, 393 Wis. 2d 629, 948 N.W.2d 877.

questions.q: What will happen next? Will anything change before the November election?
questions.a: Likely not. The rule has been blocked while the litigation continues, and the judge that blocked the rule reasoned that the states challenging will likely be successful in arguing that the rule violates the law. While it’s possible that an appeals court could disagree with the federal judge who blocked the rule, the likelihood that any court will allow the rule to go back into effect lessens as we get closer to Election Day. This is because federal courts in particular, including the U.S. Supreme Court, are usually reluctant to change the rules for voting and procedure in close proximity to an election. Nothing is guaranteed, but the Commission will provide timely updates if something changes.

questions.q: Will USPS' new postmark rules impact Wisconsin voters?
questions.a:
No. Unlike other states, Wisconsin is a “in-hand” ballot state.

Absentee ballots must be in the hands of election officials by 8 p.m. on Election Day to be counted. This means USPS postmarks on absentee ballots are irrelevant. The time when the ballot was “in hand” by the clerk’s office is what determines a ballot’s status, not the postmark on the envelope in which it was mailed.

If you’re planning to mail in your absentee ballot, the WEC recommends doing so at least 10 days before Election Day.

Voters registering to vote by mail do need to have their mail postmarked 20 days before an election, see Wis. Stat. § 6.28(1)(a) (https://docs.legis.wisconsin.gov/statutes/statutes/6/ii/28/1/a). You can also register to vote online or in person at your local clerk's office. Visit MyVote.wi.gov (https://myvote.wi.gov/en-us/) to learn more.

questions.a:
A postmark is a marking applied by the USPS to record the date, location, and zip code of where it was first processed.

questions.q: Could the electronic transmission of unofficial election results be hacked?
questions.a:
Some theories postulate that a third-party could intercept the very brief results transmission, and break the encryption, and somehow alter the data to change election results. This narrative fails to recognize many facets of the elections process. In addition to overcoming incredible technical challenges and achieving spectacularly precise timing, the theory ignores the fact that transmitted results are encrypted with a specific security key needed to pass through the voting system firewall and also ignores the fact that the tabulator results are printed on paper.

In addition, those hard copy results are further backed by paper ballots or a paper record for each and every vote. Indeed, the herculean technical feat of “hacking” the results transmission may be easily undone by a simple phone call to verify the transmission – something many Wisconsin clerks already do.

 Still have questions? Contact us.

If you couldn't find information about a topic you've been hearing about, please don't hesitate to contact WEC.

questions.q: What is a Partisan Primary and how do I avoid crossover voting?
questions.a:
Wisconsin voters can vote in a Partisan Primary to determine who they want to see on the General Election ballot. Wisconsin law allows voters to choose which political party’s primary they wish to vote in without having to register to vote with a party affiliation or designation. However, a voter may only vote within one party’s primary on the ballot.

Put simply, voters must pick a party preference when filling out a ballot for the Partisan Primary and stick with that party down the ballot when choosing their candidates of choice. If you select a party preference but vote in multiple primaries, only your chosen party’s votes will count. This is called crossover voting. Votes cast for any other party will not be counted.

If a voter does not choose a party and votes in more than one party’s primary, no votes are counted for any partisan contest.

Below outlines the Special Instructions and Party Preference sections that are printed on every ballot:

For more information on crossover voting, please see Chapter 14.22 of the Election Law & Administration in Wisconsin (ELAW) Manual (https://elections.wi.gov/elaw).

questions.q: Does crossover voting impact referendums?
questions.a: No. Referenda will not be impacted if crossover voting occurs. You can vote any way you'd like on ballot referendums.

questions.q: What should I do if I accidentally crossover voted?
questions.a:
If you crossover voted at the polls, alert a poll worker and they can issue you a new ballot.

If you crossover voted filling out your absentee ballot (and have not returned it yet), contact your municipal clerk. You can find your municipal clerk's contact information here: My Municipal Clerk (https://myvote.wi.gov/en-us/My-Municipal-Clerk).

questions.q: Could someone change my voter record or falsely obtain a ballot in my name on the MyVote Wisconsin website?
questions.a:
People cannot make changes directly to a voter’s data on the MyVote website or obtain a ballot from the site directly. People can submit a request to their municipal clerk for an absentee ballot through the site, much the same way a person can make these requests on paper or by email. Requests to receive a ballot are routed to the appropriate city, village, or town clerk for processing, see Wis. Stat. § 6.86.  (https://docs.legis.wisconsin.gov/statutes/statutes/6/iv/86)The clerk, or their assigned staff, review each request for sufficiency before approving or denying the request and sending the ballot.

Submitting a false request, either by paper or electronically, is a crime and may be subject to penalties under state and federal law. There have been several prosecutions and convictions of people falsely requesting someone else’s ballot or obtaining a ballot for a fake person or dead person. If you believe someone submitted a false request in your name, please contact your city, village, or town clerk immediately.

questions.q: Can someone find out my voting record on the MyVote Website?
questions.a:
It’s understandable that people may be concerned about someone else viewing their voter records on the MyVote Wisconsin website. MyVote only displays information that is already required by law to be public information, see Wis. Stat. § 6.36(1)(b).  (https://docs.legis.wisconsin.gov/statutes/statutes/6/ii/36/1/b)For example, the law requires the name and address of nearly all registered voters to be a public record. Likewise, a person’s voting history, polling place location, and municipal clerk information is all public. Voting history does not mean disclosing WHO you voted for. That information is kept private. Instead, voting history lists which elections you participated in.

Protected information, like a voter’s date of birth, is not available or displayed on MyVote.

Extra protection is available to some voters. Wisconsin law affords additional protection to voters who are victims of domestic abuse, sexual assault, or stalking. Judicial officers and their family members may also receive enhanced protection of their data. Voters covered by the added protection do not appear on MyVote.

More information about enhanced confidentiality is available here: https://elections.wi.gov/clerks/election-topics-z/confidential-voters. Judicial officers interested in learning more should contact the Wisconsin Court System.

questions.q: Can election results be altered by adding or subtracting votes?
questions.a:
No.

In Wisconsin, there is a paper trail for every single vote cast. That means there is a paper ballot, that represents every single vote. At every poll site, whether for in-person voting or at a central count location, the number of ballots cast must match the number of voters. If there’s any mismatch between the number of ballots cast and the number of voters, whether at the municipal or county level, the discrepancy is easy to identify and is investigated immediately.

questions.q: Could a clerk add or subtract votes to change the results of an election?
questions.a:
No. There is no possible way for a clerk to add any, yet alone hundreds or even thousands of ballots to a vote total on Election Night.

Vote totals can shift throughout the evening or days following an election – but that does not mean something went wrong. Instead, it means election officials did their jobs and made sure every valid ballot was counted. These shifts are often due to tens of thousands of absentee ballots still being processed after polls close. See more on this topic here. https://elections.wi.gov/faq?title=&field_audience_target_id=All&field_faq_type_target_id=149#accordion-13011

In addition, under the WisVote system (the system used by clerks to issue absentee ballots), clerks cannot issue absentee ballots on Election Day. The system locks out that functionality after the statutory deadline to issue absentee ballots has passed.

If someone attempted to remove a ballot from the total, they would also have to erase all the records of the person who voted. If they tried to do this in person, this means erasing the voter’s signature in the poll book, altering the count of ballots issued recorded by local poll workers, and altering the count of ballots tabulated. Doing this undetected in a room full of election officials and observers would be impossible.

Trying to remove an absentee ballot would be even more difficult, because absentee ballots have additional records in several different places within the voting database, including documenting the absentee request, the ballot delivery, and the ballot return.

Further, there is no way for the clerk to know who had voted on Election Day, which would mean any attempt to add voters and additional votes would result in documented situations of double voting.

questions.q: How is voting equipment certified in Wisconsin?
questions.a:
Equipment standards and testing information are publicly available on the Wisconsin Elections Commission website.

Before any voting system may be used in the State of Wisconsin, it must be approved in a public meeting by the bipartisan, six-member Wisconsin Elections Commission. The six-member Commission also reviews and certifies modem components of voting systems. Chapter EL 7 of Wisconsin’s Administrative Code governs the process. Voting Equipment may be accredited by the U.S. Election Assistance Commission (EAC) prior to its approval by the six-member Wisconsin Elections Commission, but EAC certification is not required for state certification in Wisconsin. Wisconsin Act 261 of 2015 eliminated the requirement that all voting systems approved for use in Wisconsin be accredited by the EAC.

questions.q: What standards must voting equipment meet?
questions.a:
Some voting equipment contains communication hardware to transmit the results to other devices. The communications (modem) component of the voting system or equipment must be tested to the requirements contained in the most recent version or versions of the Voluntary Voting System Guidelines (VVSG) currently accepted for testing and certification by the U.S. Election Assistance Commission (EAC). Compliance with the applicable VVSG may be substantiated through federal certification by the EAC, through certification by another state that requires compliance with the applicable VVSG, or through testing conducted by a federally certified voting system test laboratory (VSTL) to the standards contained in the applicable VVSG.

Voting equipment containing telecommunications components must meet stringent standards in five evaluation areas discussed below.

questions.q: How is voting equipment tested before Election Day?
questions.a:
All municipalities are required to conduct a public test of their voting equipment within 10 days prior to each election. Pre-election testing is intended to confirm the accuracy of voting equipment programming. This event is considered a public meeting and must be noticed at least 48 hours prior. The public is invited to attend and observe the testing process.

Programming is verified by feeding a set of pre-marked ballots into each machine and reviewing the results tape that is generated. Pre-determined vote totals for each candidate in a contest for the public test should differ so that any errors in a contest can be detected. An errorless count is required at the conclusion of the process. Any anomalies identified in testing must be remedied before the equipment can be used in an election. Wis. Stats. § 5.84(1)

questions.q: Is voting equipment tested after Election Day?
questions.a:
All municipalities are required to conduct a public test of their voting equipment within 10 days prior to each election. Pre-election testing is intended to confirm the accuracy of voting equipment programming. This event is considered a public meeting and must be noticed at least 48 hours prior. The public is invited to attend and observe the testing process.

Programming is verified by feeding a set of pre-marked ballots into each machine and reviewing the results tape that is generated. Pre-determined vote totals for each candidate in a contest for the public test should differ so that any errors in a contest can be detected. An errorless count is required at the conclusion of the process. Any anomalies identified in testing must be remedied before the equipment can be used in an election. Wis. Stats. § 5.84(1)

Wisconsin statutes also require a post-election audit of voting systems used in Wisconsin after each General Election. The audit is designed to assess the accuracy and performance of each voting system approved for use in the state. The audit is a public meeting and proper notice must be provided at least 48 hours in advance. A significant sample of reporting units that use each type of voting equipment are included in the selection process. The parameters of each audit are established by the Elections Commission.

During this process, election workers conduct an independent hand count of paper ballots and tally the results of the contests. The final hand-count tally total is compared to the election night voting system results. Audit materials are submitted to WEC for review. Any discrepancies or tabulator errors are investigated by WEC staff and reviewed in a public meeting of the Commission.

questions.q: How are results transmitted on election night?
questions.a:
Only unofficial results are provided on Election Night. Wisconsin does not have a statewide system for reporting unofficial results on Election Night, and there is no official central website or feed where results are reported. Instead, state law requires that counties post the unofficial Election Night numbers for each polling place. The unofficial statewide and county results that the public sees on Election Night and the days thereafter come from the news media, including the Associated Press, which collects them from the 72 county clerks’ websites.

questions.q: How does the electronic transmission of data work?
questions.a:
In the counties where results are transmitted digitally to the county, a combination of wireless and dial-up transmission are used. Regardless of the method of transmission, or whether the modems are internal or external, all transmission components are disabled until after the close of polls. During the hours in which ballots are cast by voters, there are zero tabulators in Wisconsin with network connectivity enabled. Only after the “close polls” button on the tabulator has been pressed can election inspectors attempt to transmit unofficial results.

Transmissions from the tabulator are encrypted to prevent the data from being read or altered. In addition, tabulators include extra layers of protection not seen in other secure networked communication. For example, each signal is cryptographically signed by a key established for each election and any signals not signed will be rejected by the EMS network’s security systems. The results data also has another layer of encryption that can only be decrypted by the EMS itself, after the data has reached its final destination. If an attacker tampered with these transmissions without breaking the encryption, decryption would fail and the EMS would discard the transmission. If an attacker broke the encryption, they would not be able to re-encrypt the data with the appropriate signatures and the EMS would discard the transmission.

questions.q: Could the electronic transmission of unofficial election results be hacked?
questions.a:
Some theories postulate that a third-party could intercept the very brief results transmission, and break the encryption, and somehow alter the data to change election results. This narrative fails to recognize many facets of the elections process. In addition to overcoming incredible technical challenges and achieving spectacularly precise timing, the theory ignores the fact that transmitted results are encrypted with a specific security key needed to pass through the voting system firewall and also ignores the fact that the tabulator results are printed on paper.

In addition, those hard copy results are further backed by paper ballots or a paper record for each and every vote. Indeed, the herculean technical feat of “hacking” the results transmission may be easily undone by a simple phone call to verify the transmission – something many Wisconsin clerks already do.

questions.q: Is it true that an organization called WiscNet receives election results?
questions.a:
No. Some recent claims allege that a non-profit organization called WiscNet is involved in the transmission of election results. This conclusion is based on IP address attribution. Every network endpoint is assigned an IP address by which it can be identified, and the ”owner” of these IP addresses is typically public record. However, the owner of the vast majority of IP addresses is the service provider that connects that IP address to the internet. WiscNet itself has no ability to read the encrypted results transmission. Rather, WiscNet appears providing network services for some counties receiving unofficial Election Night results.

While WEC does not have a role in managing, approving, or recommending internet service or network servicing providers used by municipalities, it appears that WiscNet has provided network services to hundreds of Wisconsin counties, municipalities, school districts, and public libraries for more than 30 years. Information about WiscNet is readily available on their website. It therefore makes perfect sense that a county IP address would appear to belong to WiscNet, in the same way a residential IP address might appear to belong to Charter Communications.

questions.q: Could a third-party have intercepted or altered election results?
questions.a:
Reasonable deduction and simple logic refute nearly all possible claims of a hack, including the following theories: whether a mysterious third-party receives unofficial election results; if a malicious algorithm was installed to switch votes; or if a hostile, foreign force obtained a connection into a tabulator before, during, or after the election.

In all of these situations a simple recount or re-tabulation, mechanically or by hand, demonstrate the theory to be inconsistent with the facts. In 2020, recounts were undertaken in both Milwaukee and Dane Counties, and post-election audits were conducted in over 180 election reporting units, and all provided verification of the original, official results. Not one of these review efforts demonstrated a material problem with the tabulators or the software.

questions.q: Do you have to be a U.S. citizen to vote in Wisconsin?
questions.a:
Yes. State and federal law prohibits noncitizens in Wisconsin from voting in state or federal elections. No municipality or jurisdiction in Wisconsin permits noncitizens to vote in any election.

Current state law, under “Qualifications, general” in Wisconsin statute § 6.02(1), says this: “Every U.S. citizen 18 or older who has resided in an election district or ward for 28 consecutive days before any election where the citizen offers to vote is an eligible voter.”

questions.q: Are noncitizens with a valid Wisconsin driver’s licenses allowed to vote?
questions.a: No. Again, in order to vote in Wisconsin, one must be a U.S. citizen. Possessing a valid Wisconsin driver’s license does not change the fact that a noncitizen is still disqualified from voting.

questions.q: What is the upcoming referendum question about?
questions.a:
In the Nov. 5, 2024, General Election, there is a statewide referendum question on the ballot regarding voter eligibility. The referendum will ask voters to choose yes or no on the following question: “Eligibility to vote. Shall section 1 of article III of the constitution, which deals with suffrage, be amended to provide that only a United States citizen age 18 or older who resides in an election district may vote in an election for national, state, or local office or at a statewide or local referendum?”

Additional information about the referendum question is available in the Type C Notice, where the Attorney General has provided an explanatory statement:

File

Type C Notice for Referendum for November 5, 2024 (https://elections.wi.gov/media/28606/download)

questions.q: How does Wisconsin prevent non-citizens from voting?
questions.a:
Voters must attest to their U.S. citizenship on their voter registration form under penalty of perjury. In addition to criminal penalties, non-citizens could face the additional penalty of deportation if convicted of a crime.

Voters are required to present valid proof of residence when registering, and most voters also need to show a photo ID each time they vote. While these registration and voting requirements do not necessarily require the voter to prove citizenship, they do present additional barriers to any noncitizens attempting to vote. Acceptable forms of ID include a Wisconsin driver license, state ID, or other specified forms but not a specific document proving citizenship.

On Nov. 1, 2024, six bipartisan members of the Wisconsin Elections Commission approved guidance to clerks on how they and their election inspectors should handle situations in which an individual in their jurisdiction presents a DMV-issued form of identification that has been marked with “Limited Term” or “Non-Domiciled.”

Both forms of identification are issued to non-citizens who are lawfully in the United States. The guidance states that if a poll worker is presented with a driver license that indicates the person at one time was a noncitizen, they should ask that voter for proof of citizenship. If the voter doesn’t have it, the voter will be asked under oath to attest to their citizenship through a challenge process sanctioned by state law. The details of the approved guidance are posted on our website  (https://elections.wi.gov/memo/election-inspector-guide-limited-term-non-domiciled-dmv-products)as a clerk communication.

Additionally, voter information in Wisconsin is cross-referenced with state databases, such as the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV), the Department of Corrections (DOC) and the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC), to confirm the accuracy of registration details, ensuring that voters meet residency and identification requirements.

Wisconsin and federal law do not provide for any process to systematically verify citizenship beyond the attestation during registration.

questions.q: How do election officials verify that a voter is a U.S. citizen?
questions.a:
The citizenship question is a part of the voter registration process. In order to become a registered voter, an applicant must attest in writing on the registration form that they are a U.S. citizen. Making a false claim of citizenship to an election official to register to vote is a felony and carries serious consequences, up to and including fines and jail time. Wis. Stats. §§ 12.13(1)(b), 12.60(1)(a), and 939.50(3)(i). Noncitizens would also potentially face deportation, loss of immigration status, and a prohibition to U.S. citizenship in the future.

The names of people who are registered to vote in Wisconsin and who participate in an election are fully open to public inspection, including by law enforcement entities.

questions.q: What happens if someone suspects that a voter is not a U.S. citizen?
questions.a: Individually, a voter’s registration status can be challenged by another elector as outlined in Wis. Stat. § 6.48. Additionally, anyone attempting to vote at an election can be challenged for cause on Election Day by an election inspector or another elector. Wis. Stats. §§ 6.92–6.95. If challenged, an individual will be required to swear an oath and will answer questions so that the individual’s eligibility to vote can be confirmed. Wis. Admin. Code §§ EL 9.01(2) and 9.02(2). If the individual refuses to take the oath, refuses to answer the questions, or if the answers indicate that the individual is not qualified, the individual will not be allowed to vote. An individual’s race, ethnicity, heritage, or English language proficiency alone, without more, cannot constitute cause to bring a challenge to an elector’s voting qualifications.

questions.q: How often do noncitizens attempt to vote in Wisconsin?
questions.a:
There is no evidence to indicate that a significant number of noncitizens have voted in previous elections or will do so in upcoming elections.
